standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.3.1, the sentence 'our assumption about finite variance was sufficient to imply that the population mean is well behaved', read with footnote 31, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 120 (PDF p. 138), paragraph after Theorem 3.3.6, and footnote 31. The mean functional $T_{\mathrm{E}}$: p. 118 (PDF p. 136)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] We omit the proof, which requires empirical process theory. The conditions for $T$ to be well behaved at $F$ are often implied by other assumptions; for instance, our assumption about finite variance was sufficient to imply that the population mean is well behaved. We will refer to these assumptions, as they apply to the functional under consideration, as the usual plug-in regularity conditions. [Footnote 31, first two sentences] We say $T$ is well behaved if it is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance. Formally, the Kolmogorov distance between two distributions $F$ and $G$ is given by the value of the largest divergence between their two CDFs, $\sup_x |F(x) - G(x)|$. [What is refuted] That finite variance of $F$ implies Hadamard differentiability at $F$, with respect to the Kolmogorov distance, of the mean functional $T_{\mathrm{E}}(G) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x dG(x)$, even when $T_{\mathrm{E}}$ is restricted to the CDFs with finite second moment. The CLT for the sample mean (Theorem 3.2.24) is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validators (adjudicated)] Let $F$ be the CDF of the distribution with mass $q_k = 2^{-(k+1)}$ at each integer $k = 0, 1, 2, ...$. Then $\sum_k q_k = 1$, $\mathrm{E}_F[X] = 1$, $\mathrm{E}_F[X^2] = 3$ and $\mathrm{Var}_F[X] = 2$. For each integer $n \ge 2$ let $H_n$ be the CDF of $X + n$ for $X \sim F$, and let $G_n = (1 - n^{-3})F + n^{-3}H_n$ and $t_n = n^{-2}$. Then: (a) each $G_n$ is a CDF with the same support $\{0, 1, 2, ...\}$ as $F$ and finite second moment; $\mathrm{Var}_{G_n}[X]$ is finite and $\mathrm{Var}_{G_n}[X] \to 2$; (b) with $h_n = (G_n - F)/t_n$, $G_n = F + t_nh_n$ and $\|h_n\|_\infty = n^2 \cdot n^{-3}\sup_x |H_n(x) - F(x)| \le \frac{1}{n} \to 0$, so $h_n \to 0$ in sup norm and $t_n \to 0$; (c) $T_{\mathrm{E}}(G_n) - T_{\mathrm{E}}(F) = n^{-3}\left((1 + n) - 1\right) = n^{-2}$, so $\frac{T_{\mathrm{E}}(F + t_nh_n) - T_{\mathrm{E}}(F)}{t_n} = 1$ for every $n$. A Hadamard derivative at $F$ is a continuous linear map $L_F$, so it would require this quotient to converge to $L_F(0) = 0$. Hence $T_{\mathrm{E}}$ is not Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance, although $F$ has finite variance.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [p. 118] For the random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, we can write the expected value of $X$ as $\mathrm{E}[X] = T_{\mathrm{E}}(F) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x dF(x)$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Hadamard differentiability with respect to the sup distance, as used by the validators; the book gives no formal definition] there is a continuous linear map $L_F$ with $\frac{T(F + t_rh_r) - T(F)}{t_r} \to L_F(h)$ whenever $t_r \to 0$, $\|h_r - h\|_\infty \to 0$ and each $F + t_rh_r$ is a CDF in the domain.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for each $n$: $\sum_{k=0}^{K} q_k = 1 - 2^{-(K+1)}$, $\sum_{k=0}^{K} kq_k = 1 - (K + 2)2^{-(K+1)}$, $\sum_{k=0}^{K} k^2q_k = 3 - (K^2 + 4K + 6)2^{-(K+1)}$; for a mixture $G = (1 - p)F + pH_L$ with $H_L$ the law of $X + L$: $\mathrm{E}_G[X] = 1 + pL$ and $\mathrm{E}_G[X^2] = 3 + p(L^2 + 2L)$; $\sup_x |G(x) - F(x)| \le p$. With $p = n^{-3}$, $L = n$: $\mathrm{E}_{G_n}[X] - \mathrm{E}_F[X] = n^{-2}$ and $\mathrm{Var}_{G_n}[X] = 3 + n^{-3}(n^2 + 2n) - (1 + n^{-2})^2$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate (dual validation, adjudicated; an external check of Wasserman 2006 is recorded in runs/P001/settle/settled.json). The witness is an exact rational family; the adjudicator's derivation restricts the functional to CDFs with finite second moment, the reading most favourable to the book. Under a weaker, non-continuous notion of derivative the sentence is not refuted by this sequence; the validators note that such a notion would not support Theorem 3.3.6.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3.3.1, the example offered for the 'usual plug-in regularity conditions', corrected: asymptotic normality of the sample mean from the Central Limit Theorem, not from Hadamard differentiability of the mean
canonical_claim.location: p. 120 (PDF p. 138), paragraph after Theorem 3.3.6. Theorem 3.2.24: p. 109 (PDF p. 127). Example 3.3.4: p. 119 (PDF p. 137)
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected passage] Replace 'for instance, our assumption about finite variance was sufficient to imply that the population mean is well behaved' by the scalar justification: for the population mean, the plug-in estimator is the sample mean (Example 3.3.4), and under finite variance $\mathrm{V}[X] > 0$ its asymptotic normality follows from the Central Limit Theorem (Theorem 3.2.24). When the functional delta method (Theorem 3.3.6) is invoked, suitable continuity, topology and tangent conditions must be specified. [Formal content] (i) For i.i.d. $X_1, X_2, ...$ with CDF $F$, finite $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu$ and finite $\mathrm{V}[X] = \sigma^2 > 0$: $T_{\mathrm{E}}(\hat F) = \overline{X}$ and $\sqrt{n}(T_{\mathrm{E}}(\hat F) - T_{\mathrm{E}}(F)) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \sigma^2)$, so the plug-in estimator of the mean is asymptotically normal in the sense of Definition 3.2.28 with $\phi = \sigma$. (ii) Finite variance of $F$ does not imply that $T_{\mathrm{E}}$ is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance: there is a CDF $F$ with finite variance and CDFs $G_n$ with finite variance such that $\sup_x |G_n(x) - F(x)|/t_n \to 0$ for a sequence $t_n \to 0$ while $(T_{\mathrm{E}}(G_n) - T_{\mathrm{E}}(F))/t_n = 1$ for all $n$ (the counterexample target for this finding).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Theorem 3.2.24, p. 109] Central Limit Theorem. Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be i.i.d. random variables with (finite) $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu$ and finite $\mathrm{V}[X] = \sigma^2 > 0$, and let $Z$ be the standardized sample mean. claim_correction.problem: The local-L2 lower-limit counterexample is correct, but the unqualified supplementary endpoint bound fails at the positive integer t=1. For one observation (X,Y), the polynomial q(x)=Y(x-1)/(X-1) when X≠1, and q(x)=Y when X=1, is a coefficient-measurable degree-at-most-one least-squares minimizer, yet q(1)=0 almost surely under the stated uniform/Gaussian law. Thus its endpoint tail probability is 0, rather than at least 1/4; this does not depend on any failure of existence or measurability. The endpoint supplement also needs separate estimator notation because the main schedule gives J_(t²)=floor(t^(3/2)), whereas the supplement uses degree t.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 4.3.9 (Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator) and the consistency claim after it, corrected with a sufficient degree-growth condition
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected definition] Definition 4.3.9. Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator. For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, X_1), (Y_2, X_2), ..., (Y_n, X_n)$, the polynomial least squares sieve estimator of the conditional expectation function is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_n[Y|X = x] = \sum_{k=0}^{J_n}\hat\beta_kx^k$, where $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{J_n+1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - \sum_{k=0}^{J_n} b_kX_i^k\right)^2$, where $J_n \to \infty$ and the degree grows slowly enough that the sample fit is stable in a population-normalized polynomial basis and the sampling noise vanishes. [One explicit sufficient version, with every hypothesis] Let $(Y_i, X_i)$ be i.i.d., let $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = [a, b]$ be a compact interval, let $m(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$ be continuous on $[a, b]$, and let $\mathrm{Var}(Y|X) \le V < \infty$. Let $p_0, ..., p_{J_n}$ be polynomials with $\deg p_k = k$ that are orthonormal in $L^2(P_X)$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[p_j(X)p_k(X)] = \mathbb{1}\{j = k\}$, let $P$ be the $n \times (J_n + 1)$ matrix with entries $p_k(X_i)$ and $G_n = P^TP/n$. If $J_n \to \infty$, $(J_n + 1)/n \to 0$, and for some fixed $c > 0$, $\Pr[\lambda_{\min}(G_n) \ge c] \to 1$, then $\int(\hat m_n(x) - m(x))^2dP_X(x) \xrightarrow{p} 0$, where $\hat m_n(x) = \hat{\mathrm{E}}_n[Y|X = x]$. The Gram condition holds if $\zeta_K^2K/n \to 0$ with $K = J_n + 1$ and $\zeta_K^2 = \sup_x\sum_{k=0}^{J_n} p_k(x)^2$. [Uniform covariates] If $X$ is uniform on a compact interval, $\zeta_K^2 \le K^2$, and $(J_n + 1)^3/n \to 0$ suffices: $\Pr\left[\|G_n - I\|_{\mathrm{op}} > \frac{1}{2}\right] \le \frac{4((J_n + 1)^3 - (J_n + 1))}{n}$.

[Theorem 4.3.2, p. 158 (PDF p. 176)] Weierstrass Approximation Theorem. Let $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous. Then, $\forall \epsilon > 0$, there exists a polynomial $p$ such that $\forall x \in [a, b]$, $|f(x) - p(x)| < \epsilon$. [Notation of the validators] $P_X$ the distribution of $X$; $\lambda_{\min}$ the smallest eigenvalue; $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ the operator norm; $L_k$ the Legendre polynomials, with $p_k(x) = \sqrt{2k + 1}L_k(2x - 1)$ orthonormal for $X \sim U(0, 1)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Exact steps of the repair proof, validators' derivation, Section 8, for each $n$] For $\epsilon > 0$ let $h$ be a polynomial with $\sup_x|m(x) - h(x)| \le \epsilon$ (Weierstrass), of degree at most $J_n$ for large $n$, with basis coefficients $b_h$. Then $\hat b = b_h + b_r + b_u$ with $b_r = (P^TP)^{-1}P^Tr$, $b_u = (P^TP)^{-1}P^Tu$, $r_i = m(X_i) - h(X_i)$, $u_i = Y_i - m(X_i)$. On $\{\lambda_{\min}(G_n) \ge c\}$: $c\|b_r\|^2 \le b_r^TG_nb_r \le \|r\|^2/n \le \epsilon^2$ and $\mathrm{E}[\|b_u\|^2|X_1, ..., X_n] \le V\mathrm{tr}(G_n^{-1})/n \le V(J_n + 1)/(cn)$; and $\|\hat m_n - m\|_{L^2(P_X)} \le \epsilon(1 + c^{-1/2}) + \|b_u\|$. For the uniform design: $\mathrm{E}\|G_n - I_q\|_F^2 = \frac{\mathrm{E}[K_J(X)^2] - q}{n} \le \frac{q^3 - q}{n}$ with $q = J + 1$ and $K_J(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{J} p_k(x)^2 \le q^2$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 5.2.8 (The ML Estimator Is Consistent for the Minimum KL Divergence Predictor), with the target defined by the KL divergence at a fixed $\mathbf{x}$, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Theorem 5.2.8. The ML Estimator Is Consistent for the Minimum KL Divergence Predictor. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector. Let $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ be i.i.d. observations of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. Then the ML estimate of $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$, $g(y, \mathbf{x}; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})$ consistently estimates the minimum Kullback–Leibler divergence approximation of $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$ among all probability distributions of the form $g(y, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t})$. That is, assuming that there exists a unique $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathrm{KL}\left[f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})\,\|\,g(\cdot, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t})\right]$, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$. [What is refuted] The displayed target: the minimizer of the KL divergence at a fixed value $\mathbf{x}$, with no expectation over the distribution of $\mathbf{X}$. The intended result, with the KL divergence averaged over $\mathbf{X}$, is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validators] Let $(X, Y)$ have joint PMF $\Pr[X = 0, Y = 0] = \frac{3}{8}$, $\Pr[X = 0, Y = 1] = \frac{1}{8}$, $\Pr[X = 1, Y = 0] = \frac{1}{8}$, $\Pr[X = 1, Y = 1] = \frac{3}{8}$, so that $\Pr[X = 1] = \frac{1}{2}$, $\Pr[Y = 1|X = 0] = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\Pr[Y = 1|X = 1] = \frac{3}{4}$. Let the model be $g(y, x; t) = t^y(1 - t)^{1-y}$ for $y \in \{0, 1\}$, with $\boldsymbol\Theta = [\frac{1}{10}, \frac{9}{10}]$. Then: (a) for a true conditional success probability $p$, $K_p(t) = \mathrm{KL}[f_{Y|X}(\cdot|x)\,\|\,g(\cdot, x; t)] = p\log\frac{p}{t} + (1 - p)\log\frac{1 - p}{1 - t}$ has $K_p'(t) = \frac{t - p}{t(1 - t)}$, so the printed target is unique at each $x$: $\arg\min_{t \in \boldsymbol\Theta} K_{1/4}(t) = \frac{1}{4}$ at $x = 0$ and $\arg\min_{t \in \boldsymbol\Theta} K_{3/4}(t) = \frac{3}{4}$ at $x = 1$; (b) for every sample the ML estimator exists, is unique and equals $\hat t_n = \mathrm{clip}_{[1/10, 9/10]}(\overline{Y})$; (c) $\mathrm{E}[Y] = \frac{1}{2}$, $\mathrm{V}[Y] = \frac{1}{4}$, and for every $\epsilon > 0$, $\Pr[|\hat t_n - \frac{1}{2}| \ge \epsilon] \le \frac{1}{4n\epsilon^2}$, so $\hat t_n \xrightarrow{p} \frac{1}{2}$; (d) with $\epsilon = \frac{1}{8}$: $\Pr[|\hat t_n - \frac{1}{4}| > \frac{1}{8}] \ge 1 - \frac{16}{n}$ and $\Pr[|\hat t_n - \frac{3}{4}| > \frac{1}{8}] \ge 1 - \frac{16}{n}$, so $\hat t_n$ converges in probability to neither printed target; (e) the averaged divergence $D(t) = \frac{1}{2}K_{1/4}(t) + \frac{1}{2}K_{3/4}(t)$ has $D'(t) = \frac{t - 1/2}{t(1 - t)}$ and unique minimizer $\frac{1}{2}$, with $D(\frac{1}{4}) - D(\frac{1}{2}) = D(\frac{3}{4}) - D(\frac{1}{2}) = \frac{1}{2}\log\frac{4}{3} > 0$; (f) if $\Pr[X = 1] = q$ with the conditional laws unchanged, the limit of the ML estimator is $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{q}{2}$ (for example $\frac{3}{8}$ at $q = \frac{1}{4}$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] Likelihood Function. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector, and assume the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. Then the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$. For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood. [Definition 5.2.7, p. 195] Kullback–Leibler Divergence for Continuous Distributions. For probability density functions $p(\cdot)$ and $q(\cdot)$, the Kullback–Leibler divergence is $\mathrm{KL}[p(\cdot)\,\|\,q(\cdot)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(t)\log\left(\frac{p(t)}{q(t)}\right)dt$. The KL divergence is defined analogously for discrete random variables, with a sum replacing the integral and PMFs replacing PDFs.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact for each $n$: the likelihood is $t^{N_1}(1 - t)^{n - N_1}$ with $N_1 = \sum_i Y_i$, and $L_n(t) = a\log t + (1 - a)\log(1 - t)$ with $a = N_1/n$ has $L_n'(t) = \frac{a - t}{t(1 - t)}$, so the unique maximizer on $[\frac{1}{10}, \frac{9}{10}]$ is the clipped $a$; $\mathrm{V}[a] = \frac{1}{4n}$; clipping onto an interval containing $\frac{1}{2}$ does not increase the distance from $\frac{1}{2}$; Chebyshev's inequality gives the bounds in (c) and (d). Also $\sup_{t \in \boldsymbol\Theta}|L_n(t) - M(t)| \le |a - \frac{1}{2}|\log 9$ with $M(t) = \frac{1}{2}\log t + \frac{1}{2}\log(1 - t)$, so the example satisfies uniform convergence, compactness, continuity and uniqueness.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate (dual validation; confirmed in part: the missing expectation is a defect of the formal display, while the prose on pp. 194 and 196 carries the averaged target). canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected statement] Theorem 5.2.8. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector. Let $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ be i.i.d. observations of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. Then, under the requisite regularity conditions for ML consistency (as in Theorem 5.2.6), assuming that there exists a unique $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\left[\mathrm{KL}\left\{f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(\cdot|\mathbf{X})\,\|\,g(\cdot, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})\right\}\right]$, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$. (When the averaged KL divergence is not finite, define $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$ as the maximizer of $\mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$.) On p. 196, 'closest (in terms of KL divergence)' and 'the KL divergence of the hypothesized distribution from the true population distribution' mean the divergence averaged over the covariate distribution. [Formal content] (i) Identity: if $C = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\left[\int f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{X})\log f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{X})dy\right]$ and $M(\mathbf{t}) = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$ are finite, then $D(\mathbf{t}) := \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{X}}\left[\mathrm{KL}\{f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(\cdot|\mathbf{X})\,\|\,g(\cdot, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})\}\right] = C - M(\mathbf{t})$, so minimizing $D$ over $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is the same as maximizing $M$ (sums replace integrals for PMFs). (ii) Consistency: let $L_n(\mathbf{t}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \mathbf{t})$ and suppose (1) $\Delta_n = \sup_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}|L_n(\mathbf{t}) - M(\mathbf{t})| \xrightarrow{p} 0$; (2) there is $\mathbf{t}_* \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that for every $\epsilon > 0$, $\delta_\epsilon = M(\mathbf{t}_*) - \sup_{\|\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{t}_*\| \ge \epsilon} M(\mathbf{t}) > 0$; (3) $L_n(\hat{\mathbf{t}}_n) \ge \sup_{\mathbf{t}} L_n(\mathbf{t}) - e_n$ with $e_n \ge 0$, $e_n \xrightarrow{p} 0$. Then $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbf{t}_*$. Compactness of $\boldsymbol\Theta$, continuity of $M$ and a unique maximizer imply (2). (iii) If the model is true at $\boldsymbol\theta$, then $D(\boldsymbol\theta) = 0$ and $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = \boldsymbol\theta$ (p. 196).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5.2.5 and Example 5.2.11: 'the product can be maximized to find the ML estimate', applied to the normal/log-normal/exponential mixture, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements] [pp. 198–199] Suppose that the distribution of $Y$ conditional on $\mathbf{X}$ can be represented as a weighted average of $M$ different parametric models, $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) = p_1g_1(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_1) + p_2g_2(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_2) + ... + \left(1 - \sum_{m=1}^{M-1} p_m\right)g_M(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_M)$, where $\boldsymbol\theta = (p_1, \boldsymbol\theta_1, p_2, \boldsymbol\theta_2, ..., p_{M-1}, \boldsymbol\theta_{M-1}, \boldsymbol\theta_M)$. Then, as before, $\prod_{i=1}^{n} g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \boldsymbol\theta)$ can be maximized to find the ML estimate of $\boldsymbol\theta$. (This can sometimes be computationally tricky.) [Example 5.2.11, pp. 199–200] $g_N(y; (\mu_N, \sigma_N)) = \frac{1}{\sigma_N\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(y - \mu_N)^2}{2\sigma_N^2}}$; $g_{LN}(y; (\mu_{LN}, \sigma_{LN})) = \frac{1}{y\sigma_{LN}\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(\log y - \mu_{LN})^2}{2\sigma_{LN}^2}}$; $g_E(y; \lambda_E) = \lambda_Ee^{-\lambda_Ey}$. Consider a mixture model that incorporates all three models: $g(y; \boldsymbol\theta) = p_Ng_N(y; (\mu_N, \sigma_N)) + p_{LN}g_{LN}(y; (\mu_{LN}, \sigma_{LN})) + (1 - p_N - p_{LN})g_E(y; \lambda_E)$, where $\boldsymbol\theta = (p_N, p_{LN}, \mu_N, \sigma_N, \mu_{LN}, \sigma_{LN}, \lambda_E)$. Figure 5.2.5 visualizes the ML estimate of this mixture model, which provides a markedly better approximation. [What is refuted] That for the displayed seven-parameter mixture, with the usual unrestricted parameter domain ($p_N, p_{LN} \ge 0$, $p_N + p_{LN} \le 1$, $\mu_N, \mu_{LN} \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma_N, \sigma_{LN}, \lambda_E > 0$), the sample likelihood has a maximizer. Theorem 5.2.6, with its regularity conditions, is not refuted, and the curve of Figure 5.2.5 is not shown to be numerically wrong. [Counterexample, from the validators] Take the sample $(y_1, y_2, y_3) = (1, 2, 3)$ and, for $\sigma > 0$, $\boldsymbol\theta_\sigma = (\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, 1, \sigma, 0, 1, 1)$ (weights $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{4}$). Then $g(1; \boldsymbol\theta_\sigma) \ge \frac{1}{2\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$, $g(2; \boldsymbol\theta_\sigma) \ge \frac{e^{-2}}{4}$, $g(3; \boldsymbol\theta_\sigma) \ge \frac{e^{-3}}{4}$, so the likelihood satisfies $\prod_{i=1}^{3} g(y_i; \boldsymbol\theta_\sigma) \ge \frac{e^{-5}}{32\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}$, which exceeds any real bound $B$ at $\sigma = \frac{C}{|B| + 1}$ with $C = \frac{e^{-5}}{32\sqrt{2\pi}}$. Every admissible parameter vector has a finite likelihood at this sample, so no admissible vector maximizes the likelihood. In general, for any $n \ge 1$ and positive observations $y_1, ..., y_n$, with $\mu_N = y_1$, $\sigma_N = \sigma$ and the other parameters as above, $\prod_{i=1}^{n} g(y_i; \boldsymbol\theta) \ge \frac{e^{-\sum_{i=2}^{n} y_i}}{2 \cdot 4^{n-1}\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma} \to \infty$ as $\sigma \to 0$.

(ii) Consistency under identification: if the model is true at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, the fitted parameter space is compact, $L(\mathbf{t}) = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$ is continuous and uniquely maximized at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, and $\sup_{\mathbf{t}}|L_n(\mathbf{t}) - L(\mathbf{t})| \xrightarrow{p} 0$, then every measurable maximizer $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$ of $L_n$ satisfies $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta^0$. (iii) Normality and efficiency under explicit regularity: assume the conditions in (ii), take a measurable ML maximizer, and suppose that $\boldsymbol\theta^0$ is interior in independent coordinates. Let $P_0$ be the true observation law. Differentiation under the integral is valid, the score $s=\nabla\log g(Y,\mathbf X;\boldsymbol\theta^0)$ has finite second moment and $\mathrm E_0[s]=0$, and $I=\mathrm E_0[ss^T]$ is positive definite. fields.statement: [Corrected sentence] Correct specification by a subset alone does not guarantee consistency or efficiency of the displayed full parameter vector. If the fitted mixture is correctly specified, its true full parameter is identifiable and interior in independent coordinates, and the conditions for ML consistency and regular information-bound efficiency hold (including nonsingular information), its ML estimator is consistent and asymptotically efficient. Freely parameterized unused components must be excluded or removed before the full-vector claim is applied. [Formal content] Let $g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} p_mg_m(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_m)$ with $p_M = 1 - \sum_{m<M} p_m$. (i) Non-identification: if distinct $\boldsymbol\theta$ and $\boldsymbol\theta'$ lie in the parameter space, have the same weights with $p_j = 0$, and differ only in $\boldsymbol\theta_j$, then $g(\cdot, \cdot; \boldsymbol\theta) = g(\cdot, \cdot; \boldsymbol\theta')$, the distribution of every sample is the same under both for every $n$, $\mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \boldsymbol\theta)] = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \boldsymbol\theta')]$, and no estimator converges in probability to $\boldsymbol\theta$ under $\boldsymbol\theta$ and to $\boldsymbol\theta'$ under $\boldsymbol\theta'$. (ii) Consistency under identification: if the model is true at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, the fitted parameter space is compact, $L(\mathbf{t}) = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$ is continuous and uniquely maximized at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, and $\sup_{\mathbf{t}}|L_n(\mathbf{t}) - L(\mathbf{t})| \xrightarrow{p} 0$, then every measurable maximizer $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$ of $L_n$ satisfies $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta^0$. (iii) Normality and efficiency under explicit regularity: assume the conditions in (ii), take a measurable ML maximizer, and suppose that $\boldsymbol\theta^0$ is interior in independent coordinates. Let $P_0$ be the true observation law. Assume that there is one measurable set $S$ with $P_0(S)=1$ on which $g(y,\mathbf x;\mathbf t)>0$ for every $\mathbf t$ in the fitted parameter space, that the log likelihoods are integrable under $P_0$, and that, for every $(\mathbf x,y)\in S$, $\mathbf t\mapsto\log g(y,\mathbf x;\mathbf t)$ is $C^2$ on a common open neighborhood of $\boldsymbol\theta^0$. Differentiation under the integral is valid, the score $s=\nabla\log g(Y,\mathbf X;\boldsymbol\theta^0)$ has finite second moment and $\mathrm E_0[s]=0$, and $I=\mathrm E_0[ss^T]$ is positive definite. Assume also that every entry of the log-likelihood Hessian is integrable throughout that neighborhood, that its population expectation $H(\mathbf t)=\mathrm E_0[\nabla^2\log g(Y,\mathbf X;\mathbf t)]$ is continuous at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, that $H(\boldsymbol\theta^0)=-I$, and that the average sample Hessians converge uniformly in probability to $H$ on that neighborhood. Then $\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}-\boldsymbol\theta^0)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,I^{-1})$. For the information-bound conclusion, additionally assume that the normalized conditional model, with a fixed covariate law and a fixed dominating measure, is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$ with score $s$. Then $I^{-1}$ is a lower bound, in the positive-semidefinite order, for the asymptotic covariance of every regular asymptotically linear estimator with a mean-zero, square-integrable influence function.

canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [Footnote 15] The bootstrap may not work as a method for computing valid confidence intervals for hot deck imputation since the bias of the estimator may converge slowly (see, e.g., Abadie and Imbens 2008), but the bootstrap standard errors are likely to adequately characterize sampling variability. [Table 6.3.1] Hot Deck Imputation: Estimate 8.538, Bootstrap SE 1.204. [What is refuted] The general assurance, read as: for nearest-neighbour hot deck imputation the difficulty with the bootstrap is confined to bias, and the bootstrap standard error is a consistent estimate of the standard error when bias is not a problem. The reported numbers 8.538 and 1.204 are not shown to be wrong. [Counterexample, from the validator] For every $n$, draw i.i.d. units as follows: $P$ is uniform on $[\frac{1}{4}, \frac{3}{4}]$; conditional on $P = p$, $R$ is Bernoulli($p$); independently of $(P, R)$, $\varepsilon$ is $+1$ or $-1$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each; $Y = 50 + \varepsilon$. Take the covariate $X = P$, so the propensity score is $p_R(X) = P$; MAR, overlap and MCAR all hold, and $\mathrm{E}[Y] = 50$. Hot deck estimator $T_n$: for each unit with $R = 0$ impute the outcome of the unit with $R = 1$ nearest in $|P|$-distance (with replacement), and take the mean of the $n$ completed outcomes ($T_n = 50$ if no unit responded). Bootstrap: draw $n$ units with replacement, recompute the matches with the known scores, and let $\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)$ be the variance of the bootstrap estimate conditional on the sample. Then: (a) $\mathrm{E}[T_n] = 50$ exactly, for every $n$ (zero bias); (b) $\lim_{n \to \infty} n\mathrm{Var}(T_n) = V = 3\log 3 - \frac{1}{4} \approx 3.0458$, so $\sqrt{n}(T_n - 50) = O_p(1)$; (c) $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathrm{E}[n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)] = V_b = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{A}{2} + B\left(2\log 3 - \frac{3}{2}\right) \approx 2.6471$, where $s = 1 - e^{-1}$, $A = \frac{2}{s} - \frac{s}{2 - s}$ and $B = \frac{3}{2s} - \frac{4 - s}{2(2 - s)}$; (d) $A < 3$ and $B < \frac{3}{2}$, hence $V_b < V$; (e) $\sup_n\mathrm{E}[(n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*))^2] < \infty$, so $n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)$ is uniformly integrable and cannot converge in probability to $V$. The ordinary bootstrap variance, and hence the bootstrap standard error, is inconsistent for an exactly unbiased, root-$n$ consistent hot deck estimator.

[Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] Stable Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] Response Propensity Function. Suppose we observe $(R_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Then the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. The random variable $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ is known as the propensity score for unit $i$. [Section 6.2.3, pp. 224–225] Hot deck imputation, using nearest-neighbor matching with the propensity score (which, for the moment, we assume is known): for each missing unit, find the observed unit that is closest on $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ and use that unit's outcome to fill in the missing outcome; the hot deck imputation estimate of $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ is the sample mean with the missing values imputed. [Section 3.4.3, p. 131] the bootstrap: take a with replacement sample of size $n$ from the sample, calculate the estimate using this bootstrap sample, repeat, and calculate the standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution of the estimator. canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements] [p. 264] However, matching estimators are not plug-in estimators, and so their properties do not operate quite as expected. For example, even if we have a consistent estimator of $p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)$, matching with estimated propensity scores is not generally root-$n$ consistent—the bias (and therefore MSE) of the estimator shrinks “too slowly” as $n$ grows large—and, thus, the usual methods for constructing confidence intervals, including the bootstrap, do not generally work.$^{13}$ [Footnote 13] See, e.g., Abadie and Imbens (2008). [p. 279, footnote 20] As with hot deck imputation, the bootstrap may not work as a method for computing valid confidence intervals for matching estimators since the bias of the estimator may converge very slowly (see, e.g., Abadie and Imbens 2008), but the bootstrap standard errors are likely to adequately characterize sampling variability. [Table 7.5.1, Matching] $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)]$: Estimate 34.732, SE 1.951; $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$: Estimate 2.009, SE 1.988. [What is refuted] The assurance, read as: for one-to-one nearest-neighbour propensity score matching the bootstrap's difficulty is a matter of bias, and its standard error is a consistent estimate of the standard error when bias is not a problem. Strong ignorability holds, the propensity score $p_D(X) = \frac{1}{4} + X$ is uniform on $[\frac{1}{4}, \frac{3}{4}]$, and outcomes are bounded. Estimated score: $\hat p_n(x) = \hat a_n + x$ with $\hat a_n = \mathrm{clip}_{[1/8, 3/8]}(\overline{D} - \overline{X})$, so $\hat a_n \xrightarrow{p} \frac{1}{4}$ and $|\hat p_n(x) - \hat p_n(z)| = |x - z|$: the estimated score gives exactly the same nearest-neighbour matches as the true score, in the sample and in every bootstrap resample. canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Suppose that we have an additional set of placebo (or negative control) variables $\mathbf{W}_i$ that we do not think we need to condition on and that are not causally affected by the treatment assignment. Then we can test the null hypothesis that $\mathbf{W}_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$. This is known as a placebo test.$^{14}$ One simple way to implement this is by performing an $F$-test. An $F$-test compares a regression of $D_i$ on $\mathbf{W}_i$ and $\mathbf{X}_i$ with a regression of $D_i$ on $\mathbf{X}_i$ alone, and asks: does adding $\mathbf{W}_i$ to the regression explain more of the remaining variation in $D_i$ than we would expect by chance? If so, then we can reject the null hypothesis that $\mathbf{W}_i$ is independent of $D_i$ conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$. [What is refuted] That the test has asymptotic size at most its nominal level under the null hypothesis $\mathbf{W}_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ (equivalently, that under this null the population coefficient on $\mathbf{W}_i$ in the linear regression of $D_i$ on $(1, \mathbf{X}_i, \mathbf{W}_i)$ is zero). The usefulness of placebo variables in general is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $X$ take the values $-1, 0, 1$ with probability $\frac{1}{3}$ each; let $Z$, independent of $X$, take the values $-1, 1$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each; conditional on $(X, Z)$ let $D \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p(X))$ with $p(x) = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}x^2$; and let $W = X^2 + \frac{1}{2}Z$. (Twelve atoms: for $x = \pm 1$, each $(x, z, d = 1)$ has probability $\frac{1}{8}$ and each $(x, z, d = 0)$ has probability $\frac{1}{24}$; for $x = 0$, each $(0, z, d = 1)$ has probability $\frac{1}{24}$ and each $(0, z, d = 0)$ has probability $\frac{1}{8}$.) Then: (a) $W \perp\!\!\!\perp D|X$ holds exactly: $\Pr[W = w, D = d|X = x] = \frac{1}{2}p(x)^d(1 - p(x))^{1-d} = \Pr[W = w|X = x]\Pr[D = d|X = x]$; the propensities are $\frac{1}{4}$ or $\frac{3}{4}$, so positivity holds; $\mathrm{Var}(W|X) = \frac{1}{4} > 0$; (b) population moments: $\mathrm{E}[X] = 0$, $\mathrm{E}[X^2] = \frac{2}{3}$, $\mathrm{E}[D] = \frac{7}{12}$, $\mathrm{E}[XD] = 0$, $\mathrm{E}[W] = \frac{2}{3}$, $\mathrm{E}[XW] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(W) = \frac{17}{36}$, $\mathrm{Cov}(W, D) = \frac{1}{9}$; the regression of $D$ on $(1, X)$ has coefficients $(\frac{7}{12}, 0)$ and residual mean square $v_R = \frac{35}{144}$; the regression of $D$ on $(1, X, W)$ has coefficients $(\frac{29}{68}, 0, \frac{4}{17})$ and residual mean square $v_F = \frac{59}{272}$; the regressor moment matrix has determinant $\frac{17}{54} > 0$; (c) under i.i.d. sampling, with $F_n = \frac{RSS_R - RSS_F}{RSS_F/(n - 3)}$: $\frac{F_n}{n} \to \frac{v_R - v_F}{v_F} = \frac{4/153}{59/272} = \frac{64}{531} > 0$ almost surely, so $F_n \to \infty$ and the test rejects with probability tending to one at every fixed level; (d) the heteroskedasticity-robust Wald statistic for the coefficient on $W$, divided by $n$, converges to $\frac{(4/17)^2}{135315/334084} = \frac{18496}{135315} > 0$, so the robust test also rejects with probability tending to one. (e) For the sample of 240 observations whose counts are 240 times the atom probabilities: $RSS_R = \frac{175}{3}$, $RSS_F = \frac{885}{17}$ and $F_{240} = \frac{5056}{177} \approx 28.6$. With potential outcomes $Y(0) = 2 + Z$ and $Y(1) = 3 + Z$, treatment is strongly ignorable given $X$ and $W$ is a pre-treatment variable.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.2.8, the regression implementation of the placebo test, corrected: valid when $\mathrm{E}[D_i|\mathbf{X}_i]$ is linear in the included regressors
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected passage] One simple way to implement this is by testing the coefficients on $\mathbf{W}_i$ in a regression of $D_i$ on $\mathbf{W}_i$ and $\mathbf{X}_i$. This is a test of the placebo null provided that, under the null, $\mathrm{E}[D_i|\mathbf{X}_i]$ lies in the linear span of the included $\mathbf{X}$ regressors (including an intercept): then conditional independence implies that the coefficients on $\mathbf{W}_i$ are zero, and a joint test of those coefficients based on a consistently estimated heteroskedasticity-robust covariance matrix, interpreted asymptotically under the usual i.i.d., moment and rank conditions, has the stated meaning. Without that specification assumption the test is a test of added linear predictive content only, and a rejection is not by itself evidence against $\mathbf{W}_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$. [Formal content] Let $D_i$ be a random variable with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$, $\mathbf{X}_i = (1, X_{[1]i}, ..., X_{[K]i})$ and $\mathbf{W}_i$ random vectors with finite second moments, and suppose the moment matrix $\mathrm{E}[(\mathbf{X}_i, \mathbf{W}_i)^T(\mathbf{X}_i, \mathbf{W}_i)]$ is invertible. If (1) $\mathbf{W}_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and (2) $\mathrm{E}[D_i|\mathbf{X}_i] = \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol\gamma$ for some $\boldsymbol\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}$, then $\mathrm{E}[D_i|\mathbf{X}_i, \mathbf{W}_i] = \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol\gamma$, and the best linear predictor of $D_i$ given $(\mathbf{X}_i, \mathbf{W}_i)$ has coefficient vector $(\boldsymbol\gamma, \mathbf{0})$: the population coefficients on $\mathbf{W}_i$ are zero. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.3: 'a failure of the positivity assumption logically implies incomplete (or “limited”) overlap', and the converse of Theorem 7.3.2 that 'can almost be stated', as printed

canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements] [p. 271] Another important issue arises relating to the positivity assumption, $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) < 1 - \epsilon$. ... We proceed by illustrating that a failure of the positivity assumption logically implies incomplete (or “limited”) overlap in the population of interest. When the positivity assumption fails, then the distributions of $\mathbf{X}_i$ for treated and control units have regions with positive probability that do not completely overlap with one another. This notion of overlap is formalized in the following definition. Definition 7.3.1. Complete Population Overlap. Let $D_i$ be a random variable with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then $D_i$ has complete population overlap with respect to $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i|D_i = 1] = \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i|D_i = 0]$. ... Theorem 7.3.2. Positivity Implies Complete Population Overlap. Let $D_i$ be a random variable with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. If $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) < 1 - \epsilon$, then $D_i$ has complete population overlap with respect to $\mathbf{X}_i$. Furthermore, the converse of this claim (that population overlap implies positivity) can almost be stated here, but requires some measure-theoretic [p. 272] conditions on support. We omit the formal proof, but provide an illustrative example in the case of a single covariate. [What is refuted] (1) That failure of the positivity assumption ($\exists\epsilon > 0$: $\epsilon < p_D(\mathbf{X}_i) < 1 - \epsilon$) implies failure of complete population overlap; (2) the converse of Theorem 7.3.2, that complete population overlap implies the positivity assumption. Theorem 7.3.2 itself is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $X_i$ take values in $\{1, 2, 3, ...\}$ with $\Pr[X_i = k, D_i = 1] = 3^{-k}$ and $\Pr[X_i = k, D_i = 0] = 2^{-(k+1)}$ for every integer $k \ge 1$. Then: (a) $\sum_{k \ge 1} 3^{-k} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\sum_{k \ge 1} 2^{-(k+1)} = \frac{1}{2}$, so this is a probability distribution with $\Pr[D_i = 1] = \Pr[D_i = 0] = \frac{1}{2}$; (b) $\mathrm{Supp}[X_i|D_i = 1] = \mathrm{Supp}[X_i|D_i = 0] = \{1, 2, 3, ...\}$: complete population overlap holds; (c) $p_D(k) = \frac{3^{-k}}{3^{-k} + 2^{-(k+1)}} = \frac{2}{(3/2)^k + 2} \in (0, 1)$ for every $k$; (d) $(3/2)^k \ge 1 + \frac{k}{2}$, so $p_D(k) \le \frac{4}{k + 6}$; for every $\epsilon > 0$, with $k = \lceil 4/\epsilon\rceil$, $p_D(k) < \epsilon$ and $\Pr[X_i = k] > 0$. Hence there is no $\epsilon > 0$ with $\epsilon < p_D(X_i) < 1 - \epsilon$: the positivity assumption fails although overlap is complete.
